children: From a one-billion 5G user target and a pending satellite spectrum framework to AI-native networks and India-made telecom equipment, the four-day congress highlighted the next phase of the country's digital expansion

India's telecom sector is looking beyond the expansion of 5G coverage towards next-generation networks, domestic technology manufacturing and new sources of revenue, as the 10th edition of India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026 brought policymakers, operators and technology companies together in New Delhi.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the congress on 8 October, highlighting India's transition from a consumer to a creator of technology. Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia set a target of connecting one billion 5G users by 2030, while stressing the need to take India's home-grown innovations and technology capabilities to global markets. The discussions also reflected a broader policy emphasis on expanding consumer choice, strengthening domestic manufacturing and preparing infrastructure for growing data demand.
Satellite Spectrum And Starlink Dispute

Satellite communications emerged as one of the most closely watched policy issues at IMC, with the government indicating that the framework for satellite spectrum pricing was nearing finalisation. Scindia said the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) and the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) were close to finalising the pricing regime for satellite communication spectrum. Starlink, Reliance Jio's satellite venture Jio Satcom and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb have received licences, but commercial services remain subject to spectrum allocation and the completion of prescribed security requirements.

Starlink Business Operations Vice President Lauren Dreyer said the company had built 20 gateway sites across India and developed India-specific security controls to keep domestic user data within the country. The infrastructure represents a step towards operational readiness, although it does not itself establish that commercial services can begin.

The developments highlighted the regulatory challenge of bringing satellite broadband into the market while meeting national security requirements and establishing the terms on which competing operators can offer services. Satellite connectivity is also expected to play a role in reaching remote areas where conventional terrestrial infrastructure remains difficult to deploy.
India Sharpens Its 6G Ambitions

Alongside 5G expansion, the congress put the development of sixth-generation mobile technology and India's role in global standardisation in focus. The government's one-billion-user target for 2030 provides a measure of the scale of the existing connectivity market, while the 6G agenda looks towards the technologies and standards that will shape the next generation of networks.

The Bharat 6G Alliance and related industry discussions covered intelligent radio access networks, autonomous network operations, spectrum, research and international collaboration. At the International Bharat 6G Symposium, agreements and research papers highlighted efforts to strengthen cooperation between Indian and international technology organisations.

The wider discussion was not limited to faster connectivity. AI-native networks, edge computing, network automation and programmable infrastructure are emerging as part of the transition towards 6G. These capabilities could allow operators to manage networks more autonomously and support services that require differentiated connectivity and real-time processing.
AI Moves Into Network Infrastructure

AI was a recurring theme across the congress, with technology companies demonstrating how it could be integrated into network operations, enterprise services and connected devices. The focus was on moving beyond AI as a standalone application towards infrastructure capable of supporting automated decisions, industrial applications and more responsive digital services.

Ericsson's showcase covered AI-enabled networks, programmable network APIs, 5G Standalone capabilities and technologies designed for the transition towards 6G. Its demonstrations included AI smart glasses, connected-stadium experiences and collaborative robots using edge intelligence. The company also showcased 5G KAVACH, demonstrating how 5G connectivity can support India's indigenous automatic train protection system through reliable, real-time communications.

HCLTech presented AI-powered platforms and engineering solutions for autonomous networks, network cloudification, service assurance, Open RAN engineering and network monetisation. The focus was on helping telecom operators integrate AI into operations and improve the management of increasingly complex networks.

Tata Elxsi, meanwhile, showcased its TETHERAero platform at the GSMA Pavilion. The platform explores how 5G, network APIs and AI can support aerial mobility and autonomous mission coordination for unmanned aerial vehicles and electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft. The demonstration illustrated how telecom infrastructure could enable services beyond traditional mobile connectivity.

Together, these showcases reflected a shift in the industry's priorities. As operators invest in network expansion, the next challenge is to turn improved infrastructure into commercially viable enterprise applications and differentiated consumer services.
Made-In-India Equipment Targets Global Markets

Domestic manufacturing and exports formed another important strand of the event. Ericsson announced that antennas manufactured in India would be exported to Europe and other international markets, expanding the country's role in the company's global manufacturing and supply chain.

The company said it had produced more than 15,000 antennas and 25 million components in India since July 2025. The antennas support 5G Standalone and AI-ready networks, positioning local manufacturing as part of the industry's preparation for future network requirements.

The announcement is significant as India seeks to move beyond deploying imported technology towards developing domestic capabilities in equipment, components, research and intellectual property. It also aligns with the broader ambition of building a telecom manufacturing ecosystem that can serve both the domestic market and international customers.

A report released by KPMG in India at IMC, titled ‘The Power Beneath Connectivity: India's Path to Telecom Technology Leadership ', highlighted the economic opportunity as well as the challenges. The report projected India's telecom equipment market to grow from USD 25 billion in FY25 to USD 50 billion by FY32.

It also estimated that mobile network traffic would rise by approximately 17 per cent annually between 2025 and 2030, while telecom operator revenues would grow by 2.7 per cent a year. The gap underscores the need for operators to improve network efficiency and develop new revenue streams, even as data consumption continues to increase.

KPMG identified AI, semiconductors, cloud infrastructure and advanced manufacturing as critical areas for investment. It also called for stronger domestic research, intellectual property creation and hardware capabilities to help India capture more value across the telecom technology chain.
Standards Pavilion Shows Practical Applications

The TSDSI Standards Pavilion connected the standards discussion with applications across multiple sectors. Its demonstrations covered next-generation broadcasting and 5G, 6G-related research, IoT-based smart farming, unmanned aircraft traffic management and connected vehicles.

These applications illustrated how communications standards can support areas such as agriculture, transport and industrial operations. They also highlighted the relationship between domestic research and the development of technologies that can be deployed at scale.

The event's wider exhibition extended into smart mobility, stadium experiences, industrial robotics and transport technology. Such applications are increasingly dependent on reliable connectivity, low latency, computing at the network edge and the ability to exchange data securely.

The Department of Telecommunications also showcased initiatives linked to rural development and digital safety, including Samridh Gram, Sanchar Saathi and the Financial Fraud Risk Indicator. These programmes connect the infrastructure agenda with efforts to expand digital access and address risks associated with growing reliance on connected services.
Digital Safety Remains A Policy Priority

The expansion of digital services has also increased the importance of cybersecurity, fraud prevention and safeguards against emerging threats. Modi called for stronger protections against deepfakes and evolving cyber risks, placing digital trust alongside connectivity and innovation in the country's technology agenda.

The Financial Fraud Risk Indicator was among the initiatives highlighted in the wider digital-safety discussion. The system is designed to help identify mobile numbers associated with suspected financial fraud and support risk mitigation. Its inclusion reflects the growing role of telecom infrastructure in preventing fraud that crosses the boundaries between communications networks and financial services.

The broader policy challenge is to ensure that the expansion of AI, digital public infrastructure and connected devices is accompanied by security measures that protect users without undermining the availability of services.
The Commercialisation Challenge

Beyond government policy and large-company demonstrations, IMC provided a platform for startups, researchers and innovators to present applications built around 5G and emerging technologies. The event included startup programmes, technology demonstrations and investor interactions intended to connect new ideas with commercial opportunities.

The challenge for India is to turn these efforts into products and services that can scale beyond demonstrations. That will require investment in research and development, access to computing and manufacturing capabilities, collaboration between operators and technology companies, and a clearer path from pilot projects to commercial deployment.

The congress brought these priorities together under the theme of scaling digital technology. India's next phase of telecom growth will depend not only on expanding coverage, but also on its ability to develop indigenous technologies, strengthen the manufacturing ecosystem, improve network economics and create new connectivity applications.
